title: Logan County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Logan County wells have a median depth of 88 ft and typical yields around 15 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your land.
h1: Water wells in Logan County, Colorado
intro_html: Logan County sits on the plains with a mix of shallow alluvial and bedrock wells plus some Ogallala production. Depths and yields are generally favorable, but they vary a lot across the county. If you’re looking at land near Sterling, Fleming, Peetz, or out in the country, it helps to know what nearby wells are actually doing before you budget for drilling or buy a property.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Logan County
sections.html:
Across Logan County, the median well depth is 88 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 60 and 180 feet. About 56% of wells are under 100 feet and another 31% are between 100–300 feet. Only 2% go deeper than 600 feet, even though the deepest well on record hits 3,230 feet.

For a new domestic or stock well, most drillers will probably bid assuming something in that 60–180 foot range unless your specific spot has a history of deep holes. In areas using the Ogallala or thicker alluvium you may see moderate depths, while fractured bedrock locations can swing shallow or quite deep. Checking nearby permits around places like Atwood, Iliff, or Merino is worth the time before you write an offer.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Countywide, reported production is strong. The median tested yield is 15 gpm, and the middle half of wells report between 15 and 20 gpm. Only 2% of wells come in between 1–5 gpm, and there are 0% under 1 gpm. A full 81% of wells report at least 15 gpm.

For a single home on an exempt well, 15 gpm is more than enough for normal household use and modest irrigation inside the state’s pumping limits. Stock and small irrigation wells in the county also benefit from these higher yields. The main takeaway is that low-producing holes are relatively uncommon in Logan County, but you still want a proper yield test to confirm what your specific well will do over time.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Where it’s been measured, the median static water level in Logan County is about 44 feet below ground, with the middle half between 16 and 131 feet. That’s generally a comfortable pumping lift for standard submersible pumps.

The decade-by-decade medians move around: about 20 feet in the 1950s, 18 feet in the 1960s, then down to 62 feet in the 1970s and back up to 32 feet in the 1980s. The 2000s sit around 27 feet, but the 2010s and 2020s show deeper medians of 60 and 73 feet. That suggests water in some areas is being drawn from deeper over time. When you’re evaluating land, compare your parcel’s recent measurements to older nearby wells to see if there’s been a local drop.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how permitting has changed
sections.html:
Logan County has 9,230 wells in the state records, with 5,887 noted as constructed and 6,364 reporting a total depth. Drilling peaked in the 2000s with 1,423 permits, after a steady climb from 313 in the 1950s and 684 in the 1960s. The 1990s saw 1,281 permits. Activity has tapered some since, with 881 in the 2010s and 460 so far in the 2020s, and permits running through 2026.

Most wells are in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers (8,295 wells), with smaller numbers in the Ogallala (414) and alluvial deposits (208). The busiest drillers on record are Stewart Drilling Co. with 1,240 wells, Leslie George Canfield with 704, and M&S Drilling, Inc. with 480. That history means there’s usually a good cluster of nearby logs to study before you commit to drilling.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Logan County
sections.html:
The county sits on alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, so drilling conditions are fairly predictable. Typical drilling rates run about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 88 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out in the $3,100–$4,800 range.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a typical finished domestic well in Logan County runs roughly $9,100–$16,800, assuming no special treatment or very deep hole. If your area trends toward the 180-foot end of the "middle half" range, you’ll want to scale the per-foot drilling costs up accordingly when you budget.

sections.heading: Risks to check: water quality, dry holes, and siting
sections.html:
Out of the county’s wells, about 50% are domestic or household and 33% are stock, with 15% for irrigation and 10% for monitoring. That mix means a lot of groundwater is in daily use. Within about 10 miles of parts of Logan County there are 23 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, so a full water-quality test panel is important, not just basic bacteria and hardness.

Low-yield wells are statistically uncommon here, but fractured bedrock can still surprise you. Also make sure there’s room to meet setback distances between your well, septic system, and buildings. Before you buy, compare your parcel to nearby wells around Sterling, Crook, or Padroni to see typical depths, aquifers, and water levels.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Logan County
sections.html:
Logan County’s numbers are generally in your favor: a median depth of 88 feet, strong yields around 15–20 gpm, and a lot of well history to look at. With 8,295 wells in fractured bedrock and additional Ogallala and alluvial wells, conditions can still vary from one quarter section to the next.

For a vacant parcel, pull the state well permits around your exact spot and pay close attention to the middle half depth range of 60–180 feet and the recent static levels in the 2010s–2020s. On existing homes, ask for the original completion report and any recent flow or water-quality tests. Tie all that back into your lender’s and county’s requirements before you finalize your build or purchase plans.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Logan County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Logan County, the median well depth is about 88 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 60 and 180 feet. Around 56% of wells are under 100 feet, another 31% are between 100–300 feet, and only 2% go deeper than 600 feet. That makes most domestic and stock wells relatively shallow compared with many other parts of Colorado.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Logan County, CO?
faq.a: Reported yields here are generally strong. The median yield is 15 gpm, and the middle half of wells produce between 15 and 20 gpm. About 81% of wells report 15 gpm or more, while only 2% fall in the 1–5 gpm range and none are under 1 gpm. For a single household, 15 gpm is typically more than adequate when managed properly.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Logan County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Logan County has 23 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations within about 10 miles of some areas, so testing matters. Before relying on a well for drinking water, have it lab tested for bacteria, nitrates, metals, and PFAS where relevant, and review any historic monitoring-well data nearby.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Logan County, CO?
faq.a: Typical drilling in Logan County runs about $35–$55 per foot in local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the county’s median depth of 88 feet, the drilled hole alone usually costs around $3,100–$4,800. A complete domestic setup with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is often in the $9,100–$16,800 range, depending on depth and site conditions.

faq.q: Which aquifers do wells use in Logan County, Colorado?
faq.a: Most wells in Logan County are completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 8,295 wells recorded there. There are also 414 wells in the Ogallala aquifer and 208 in alluvial deposits. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded. Aquifer type can affect depth and water-level trends, so it’s worth checking the permits for nearby wells to see what they’re completed in.
